narrative:
The model estimated a 36.0% probability that you would be a bad credit risk, which is high enough under the lender’s risk cutoff to deny the application. This does not mean default is certain; it means the model judged the risk above what this bank accepts.

The strongest factor behind the decision was your checking account status, specifically a balance in the 0–200 DM range. Among approved applicants, this category is less common than having no stated account issue, and it was the main factor pushing the prediction toward bad credit. The second most influential factor was your one year at your present residence. Although this is shorter than the approved applicants’ average of about three years, in your case it worked in your favor and reduced the assessed risk. The third factor was the requested loan duration of 12 months, compared with an approved average of about 19 months; this shorter repayment period also worked in your favor.

So the denial was driven mainly by the checking account picture, while the shorter residence history and shorter loan term helped offset that risk. Next, ask the lender what specific account balance or history would improve your eligibility. Strengthening your checking account record, providing proof of stable income, and asking whether a guarantor or co-applicant would be accepted are practical next steps before reapplying.
